claims.text: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 exhibits a large magnetocaloric and barocaloric response.
(MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 has a brittle microstructure with poor crack resistance and load-bearing integrity.
Tailored thermomechanical processing can induce in-situ precipitation of 1–3 wt% of a Ti-rich intermetallic secondary phase in this alloy.
The induced Ti-rich secondary phase will form fine precipitates preferentially at grain boundaries.
The Ti-rich intermetallic precipitates will be ductile.
Introducing a minor secondary-particle phase can improve the load-bearing properties of a high-entropy-alloy matrix.
The Ti-rich grain-boundary precipitates will arrest or deflect cracks.
The precipitates will absorb local stress concentrations and increase grain-boundary plastic deformation.
The low secondary-phase fraction will minimally perturb the energetics of the caloric phase transition in the bulk matrix.
The intervention will improve fracture toughness by more than 20% relative to the unchanged alloy.
The intervention will increase ductility relative to the unchanged alloy.
The treated alloy will retain at least 95% of the original magnetocaloric and barocaloric effects.
The usable magnetic-field, pressure-field, temperature, and mechanical-loading boundaries will remain effectively unchanged.
A controlled comparison will use an unchanged alloy and an alloy containing 2 wt% Ti-rich secondary phase.
The hypothesis is falsified if caloric performance decreases by more than 5% or fracture-toughness improvement is less than 20%.

contradictions.description: The intervention specifies in-situ precipitation produced by tailored thermomechanical processing, whereas the experiment describes an 'added 2 wt% Ti-rich secondary phase' and says both groups receive identical processing. It is unclear whether the test changes composition, processing, or both, so it may not test the stated intervention.
